newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine bond rally seen breaking new ground.
newsitem.headline: Argentine bond rally seen breaking new ground.

text.p: Despite increasing calls by traders for a shake-out in Argentine bonds, analysts say the market's fundamentals look strong and should carry the January rally further still.

"Barring any major upsets in the U.S. Treasury market -- which we think unlikely -- the rally should remain strong, pulling spreads towards our three-month forecasts," said Esteban Thomsen, economist at ING Barings.
According to the J.P. Morgan Brady Bond Index, Argentine bonds have risen 5.80 percent in the year to date.
And, analysts say, that rise is not without reason.
"Fundamentals are good -- I see nothing upsetting those in coming months," Thomsen added.

For the Argentine Brady Floating Rate Bond (FRB), Thomsen has a three-month spread target of 330 basis points over U.S. Treasuries, compared with the current 360 basis points. Over 12 months, he is targetting 290 basis points.
"I think current bond price levels are sustainable. If there is a correction, it will just be technical," said Marina Kessler, a bond analyst at Banco Frances.

Mainly, there has been increasing evidence that the recovery that started last year is deepening. And, as shown by January's high tax collection figures, that higher growth should benefit the fiscal deficit, which should in time lead to less debt supply.
Last week, the Economy Ministry announced January tax collection at $4.36 billion, higher than expected by analysts, and boding well for for government revenues through the year.

Inflation, which generally accompanies better economic growth, is not considered a problem in Argentina or to its bonds. After the hyperinflation of the late 1980s, price pressures were definitely laid to rest by the Convertibility Plan of 1991, and moderate inflation barely ruffles Argentine traders. Last year, inflation was 0.1 percent.
Another factor traders said was a concern was Argentina's large financing requirement this year. But, "investors are feeling increasingly confident with the financing strategy," said Thomsen.
Argentina has already issued $5.5 billion in bonds of a total $8.5 billion slated for issuance in the international markets this year to cover 1997 spending needs.
Perhaps the most important engine for a continuation of the rally, however, are high international liquidity levels that have fuelled large cash inflows to emerging markets.

"There could only be a significant correction if there was a surprise in U.S. rates," said an analyst at a foreign bank who did not wish to be named. He pointed out that profit-taking has only been sporadic and the market has been able to absorb it.
